prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the distribution users believe it is serving. The paper frames this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, “Model Equality Testing,” and proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, especially a simple Hamming kernel over completions. The empirical study includes both controlled simulations against quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model swaps, and an audit of 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models. Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and unusually concrete in its attempt to turn vague concerns about API faithfulness and drift into a statistically grounded auditing procedure. The work is also commendably actionable: it releases code and data, and the experiments are designed around realistic black-box access constraints.

The main strengths are the problem formulation, the practical methodology, and the empirical findings. The formulation is clean: users often only have sample access, not logits or weights, and the paper correctly identifies that benchmark accuracy under greedy decoding is too narrow a notion of equivalence for many applications. Casting the problem as testing equality of prompt-conditional completion distributions is natural and useful. The choice to use kernel two-sample tests is also sensible, since the challenge is not merely high dimensionality but the need for a similarity notion over structured outputs. The empirical result that a very simple Hamming kernel works well in low-sample regimes is valuable, especially because it is computationally cheap and easy to explain. The API audit itself is compelling and likely to attract attention: finding that 11 of 31 endpoints differ from released reference weights is a strong practical demonstration of the framework’s relevance.

I also appreciated that the paper does not oversell exact identification. It is careful to say that the Hamming MMD induces a pseudometric and may fail to separate some distributions, and it positions the method as a practical test with good power against common distortions rather than a universally optimal solution. The discussion of effect sizes via estimated MMD, and the observation that some provider deviations are as large as swapping in a different model family, is particularly striking. This goes beyond binary hypothesis testing and gives the work more diagnostic value.

That said, I have several concerns, mostly around statistical validity under the actual experimental protocol, the semantics of the chosen kernel, and the interpretation of the API audit results.

My biggest concern is that the paper’s practical decision rule for the API audit departs from the standard hypothesis testing setup in a way that makes the reported “fail/pass” outcomes harder to interpret statistically. The paper says tests are conducted at level alpha = 0.01 using N = 10m samples, then repeated over ten samples, and endpoints “fail” if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This is no longer a single level-controlled test in the classical sense; it is a meta-procedure over repeated tests. I do not see a formal argument that this aggregate rule controls type I error at any stated level. In fact, depending on dependence across repeated draws and the finite-sample calibration of each constituent test, the effective false positive rate of the endpoint-level decision could differ substantially from 0.01. Since the headline result is “11 out of 31 endpoints are different,” the statistical meaning of that statement matters a lot. At minimum, the paper should report endpoint-level uncertainty or calibrate this repeated-testing rule under null simulations. More ideally, it should define a single test statistic aggregated across repetitions and calibrate that directly.

Relatedly, the composite null handling in Section 5 is conservative but somewhat awkward. The rule “reject only if both p1 and p2 are below alpha” does indeed upper bound the false positive rate under the union null, but it is not obvious that fp32 and fp16 are the right or sufficient nulls for “faithful implementation.” Providers may differ due to tokenizer normalization, stop-token handling, system prompts, safety layers, or decoding stack details that are not well captured by the notion “equal to either fp32 or fp16 Meta weights.” In other words, the paper’s operational null is narrower than the broader claim “which model is this API serving?” This is not fatal, but the conclusions should be phrased more carefully as “different from our chosen reference implementations under our prompting and decoding setup,” not necessarily “serving a different model” in a stronger ontological sense.

A second major issue is the dependence of the test semantics on the kernel, especially the Hamming kernel. The paper acknowledges that Hamming MMD is only a pseudometric, but the implications are deeper than the discussion suggests. The Hamming kernel effectively emphasizes token-position agreement and entropy-like changes in local output patterns. This makes it well suited to detecting certain distortions, such as watermarking or reduced diversity, but it may miss semantically meaningful changes that preserve local token overlap, or conversely flag changes that are operationally unimportant for a user’s task. The paper partly addresses this by correlating MMD with HumanEval accuracy, but the correlation is only moderate. I think the paper should more explicitly distinguish “distributional non-equivalence under this kernel” from “meaningful user-facing model substitution.” Right now, some of the prose around provider deviations risks conflating the two.

This concern is especially relevant because the prompt distributions used in the main simulations are somewhat synthetic. The Wikipedia continuation task uses random 100-character strings from multilingual Wikipedia and asks for continuation. This is a convenient long-form generation benchmark, but it is not obvious that it reflects the prompt distributions of typical API users, especially for instruction-tuned chat models. The paper does include HumanEval and UltraChat in the API audit, which helps, but the controlled power studies in Section 4 are still centered on this synthetic continuation setup. I would have liked to see stronger evidence that the Hamming kernel remains the best choice across more realistic prompt distributions, including multi-turn chat, retrieval-augmented prompts, or code editing tasks. As written, the empirical claim “Hamming MMD is powerful for this task” is well supported for the chosen tasks, but perhaps not yet broadly enough for the generality implied by the framing.

A third concern is about the fairness and reproducibility of the API comparisons. Black-box APIs often differ in undocumented but consequential ways: tokenizer versions, chat templates, hidden system prompts, stop sequence defaults, max token truncation behavior, repetition penalties, top-p defaults, and safety filtering. The paper says it explicitly requested temperature 1 and compares in character space when tokenizers differ, which is good, but many other sources of mismatch remain. Some of these are arguably part of “the distribution the API is serving,” so detecting them is legitimate. However, if the goal is to infer whether the provider modified the underlying model weights or inference stack relative to Meta’s release, then these confounds matter. For example, a provider could wrap the same base model in a different chat template and be flagged. That may still be useful from a user perspective, but it is a different claim than undisclosed quantization or finetuning. The paper should disentangle these interpretations more carefully and perhaps include ablations showing sensitivity to prompt formatting and API parameterization.

On the statistical side, I would also like more detail on calibration and power under finite samples. The paper estimates p-values by simulating the null from P in Section 4, and mentions permutation as an alternative. For the API setting, where P is itself estimated from finite samples from a local implementation, there are several practical questions. How stable are p-values across random seeds and prompt subsets? How much does the test depend on the quality of the local reference implementation and hardware/software stack? If the local fp32/fp16 implementation differs from Meta’s intended reference due to library versions or sampling implementation, then the audit may partly measure local-reference mismatch rather than provider mismatch. This is especially important because the paper’s motivating claim is about auditing third-party APIs against released weights. In practice, “released weights” do not define a unique distribution without a precise inference stack.

I also found some aspects of the empirical evaluation slightly selective. The Hamming kernel is compared against all-substrings, one-hot, and two multinomial tests, which is a reasonable baseline set, but there are other natural alternatives that seem missing. For example, edit-distance-inspired kernels, n-gram kernels with tunable lengths, embedding-based kernels over completions, or tests on summary statistics such as length, entropy proxies, or lexical diversity could be competitive in low-sample regimes. Since the paper’s main methodological claim is that a simple Hamming kernel is especially effective, a broader baseline comparison would strengthen that claim. Similarly, the paper focuses on MMD, but energy distance or classifier two-sample tests might be relevant baselines, especially in character space.

Another limitation is that the paper does not fully characterize what kinds of differences are undetectable or hard to detect. The fp16 result already hints at blind spots. More generally, because the kernel is positionwise, changes that preserve marginal token identities at each position while altering higher-order dependencies may be difficult to detect. It would be useful to include adversarial or constructed alternatives illustrating failure modes. This would help users understand when a non-rejection should not be overinterpreted as evidence of equality.

The effect-size interpretation via MMD is interesting but should be handled with care. Comparing an API-reference MMD value to the MMD between two entirely different model families is intuitively appealing, but because the Hamming MMD is kernel-dependent and prompt-distribution-dependent, these comparisons are not absolute. A value of 0.03 on one task does not necessarily mean the same thing on another task or under another kernel. The paper mostly respects this, but some of the language around “further from the reference than substituting an entirely different model” could be read too strongly. I would recommend emphasizing that this is relative to the chosen prompts, decoding settings, and kernel.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The problem is real, the framing is elegant, and the empirical audit is novel and useful. The work is likely to stimulate follow-up research on black-box model auditing, distribution shift detection for generative APIs, and better kernels or tests for structured outputs. I also think the release of a dataset and package increases the paper’s practical value.

For improvement, I would strongly encourage the authors to do the following. First, formalize and calibrate the endpoint-level decision rule used in the API audit. If repeated testing over ten draws is retained, provide null simulations showing the effective false positive rate and perhaps confidence intervals on rejection frequencies. Second, clarify the scope of the claims: the method detects distributional differences under a chosen prompt distribution and kernel, not necessarily weight-level substitution. Third, add more realistic and diverse prompt distributions to the controlled power study, ideally including chat-style prompts and code tasks, to support the generality of the Hamming-kernel recommendation. Fourth, expand the baseline set to include at least one embedding-based or classifier-based two-sample test and perhaps a simpler lexical-statistics baseline. Fifth, discuss more explicitly the role of inference-stack confounds and local reference implementation choices in the API audit.

I also have a few smaller comments. The notation is mostly clear, but the paper sometimes slides between testing equality of conditional distributions P(.|x), equality of joint distributions under pi, and equality of “models” in a looser sense; tightening this language would help. The use of random 100-character Wikipedia prefixes across multiple languages is interesting, but I would like more justification for why this is a good stress test for instruction-tuned models. The computational cost of the all-substrings kernel is mentioned as expensive, but some runtime comparisons would be useful. Finally, since the paper emphasizes user-facing auditing, it would be helpful to provide practical guidance on how users should choose prompts pi for their own applications and how many samples are needed for a desired power level.

In summary, this is a strong and thought-provoking paper with clear practical relevance and a solid core idea. Its main weakness is not the basic methodology, but the gap between the clean statistical formulation and the messier endpoint-level audit protocol and interpretation. With stronger calibration of the final decision rule and more careful framing of what exactly is being detected, this could be a very impactful contribution.

My overall assessment is positive. I lean toward acceptance if the venue values practical, empirically grounded work on LLM auditing, though I think the statistical interpretation of the API audit results should be tightened before publication.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formalizes auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, termed Model Equality Testing, where one compares samples from an API against samples from a reference model distribution under matched prompts and decoding settings. The main methodological proposal is to use MMD-based two-sample tests with string kernels, especially a simple Hamming kernel over completions, to detect distributional deviations caused by quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model substitution, or temporal drift. Empirically, the authors compare several kernels and multinomial tests in simulation, finding the Hamming-MMD test to have the best small-sample power in their setup, and then apply it to 31 commercial Llama API endpoints, reporting that 11 differ significantly from Meta reference weights. The paper also uses estimated MMD values as effect-size proxies to compare models and providers.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: users increasingly rely on black-box LLM APIs and often cannot verify whether the served model matches the advertised one.
Provides a clean statistical formalization of API auditing as a two-sample testing problem, which is conceptually appealing and broadly applicable.
The use of MMD is well motivated for high-dimensional structured outputs, and the decomposition with prompt-conditioned kernels is elegant.
The empirical study is fairly extensive: multiple distortions (quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps), multiple open and closed models, and a real-world audit of commercial endpoints.
The proposed Hamming kernel is simple, computationally efficient, and appears practically effective in the low-sample regime considered.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by also estimating pairwise distances/effect sizes between models and APIs.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset improves reproducibility and practical impact.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical claims rely heavily on one specific kernel and a narrow family of prompt distributions; there is limited theoretical justification for why Hamming similarity should be broadly optimal beyond the tested settings.

The paper does not sufficiently disentangle true model-distribution differences from implementation-level differences such as tokenizer handling, stop-sequence behavior, hidden system prompts, safety filters, server-side prompt templating, or undocumented decoding defaults, especially in the commercial API audit.

The audit conclusions may overstate what is being detected: rejection only shows a distributional difference under the tested prompt distribution and decoding setup, not necessarily that the provider is serving a different underlying model in a substantive sense.

Power and type-I calibration are not characterized rigorously for the practical protocol used in the API audit, which includes repeated tests, averaging rejection rates over ten runs, and composite-null decisions.

The evaluation is mostly empirical and lacks stronger baselines from modern sequence/distribution comparison methods, such as embedding-based kernels, classifier two-sample tests, or token-level likelihood-ratio style approaches when logits are available for open models.
The use of random Wikipedia continuations as the main simulation task may not reflect many realistic user workloads, and the generalization claims across tasks are limited.

Some conclusions drawn from estimated MMD magnitudes, such as being 'further than another model family,' are interesting but may be sensitive to kernel choice and prompt distribution, which weakens interpretability.
methodological_flaws: The paper's central test with the Hamming kernel is based on a pseudometric, not a characteristic kernel. Therefore MMD=0 does not imply equality of distributions. While the authors acknowledge this, some framing occasionally blurs the distinction between testing equality and testing equality under a coarse feature map. In principle, there can be false negatives against meaningful distribution shifts that preserve the chosen features.

The API audit protocol departs from a standard level-alpha hypothesis test: tests are repeated over ten independently collected samples and an endpoint is declared failed if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. The paper does not provide a formal proof that this aggregate decision rule preserves the advertised false positive rate, nor an empirical calibration study for this exact protocol.

For the composite null over fp32 or fp16 references, the conjunction rule p1<alpha AND p2<alpha does control FPR by a simple union/intersection argument, but the practical setting likely involves dependence between p-values because the same API samples and prompts are reused. The proof sketch is informal and does not fully discuss dependence or finite-sample calibration under the simulated-p-value procedure.

The empirical p-values are obtained by simulating the null from the reference model P. This assumes the local implementation of the reference model exactly represents the intended null distribution, including tokenizer, sampling algorithm, randomization, and stopping behavior. Any mismatch here can induce apparent rejections unrelated to provider-side model modification.

Character-space comparison across APIs with different tokenizers is pragmatic, but it changes the estimand relative to token-space model equality. Two APIs could implement the same conditional distribution over semantic outputs yet differ in formatting or whitespace conventions and be flagged; conversely, token-level differences may be obscured after decoding.

The claim that some providers may have 'substituted an entirely different language model' is not directly supported by the test. Large MMD under one kernel and prompt distribution does not identify the cause of deviation and cannot distinguish substitution from decoding changes, safety layers, prompt wrappers, or output post-processing.

The correlation analysis between HumanEval accuracy differences and MMD is descriptive only and based on a modest R^2. It should not be interpreted as validating MMD as a proxy for capability differences in general.

The simulation study reports power over 100 Monte Carlo runs and multiple prompt distributions, but there is limited reporting of uncertainty for endpoint-level audit decisions and no ablation on sensitivity to temperature mismatch, prompt formatting, stop tokens, or API nondeterminism, all of which are crucial for real-world validity.
